articles.title: ‘Weak and dizzy’: the secretive ICE force-feeding tactics that ended a Cuban father’s hunger strike
articles.author: José Olivares
articles.body_markdown:
The text message that came from inside the Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention center was stark: “I have spent five days eating regular food. If I don’t eat it, they put the tube in me to feed me.”

A Cuban asylum seeker, Luis Alejandro Cora Pérez, 32, said in messages to the Guardian this month that he was still weak and dizzy after three months without eating, but that he had broken his hunger strike because being force-fed was just too painful.

The Trump administration responded to requests for comment by denying it had force-fed Cora Pérez. But the detainee sent more details – and his is far from an isolated case.

Cora Pérez was one of two men on hunger striker at a Texas facility for whom ICE sought and received a federal judge’s permission to force-feed in recent weeks, a Guardian investigation found.

Cora Pérez and the other man were locked up inside the Port Isabel service processing center, an ICE detention facility in south Texas, just a few miles from the US-Mexico border, on the coast near where Elon Musk’s SpaceX launches rockets. Cora Pérez began a hunger strike in August to protest against his prolonged detention by federal immigration officials while his case plays out. At first he only drank water, then after three weeks, he says he began to drink one Ensure nutritional shake per day.

On 30 October, court records show ICE received permission to forcibly feed and hydrate him, and to restrain him while doing so.

The next day he says six guards at the center held him down, while medical staffers inserted a feeding tube through his nose and down his throat, and pumped nutritional liquid into his stomach – a process he called “traumatizing, both physically and psychologically”.

On 3 November, ICE then received permission from a federal judge to force-feed another hunger striker at Port Isabel, from Uzbekistan, federal court records show. The DHS says the Uzbek man has not been subjected to the practice, however.

On Wednesday night, after weeks of communications, Cora Pérez was suddenly transferred to another detention center in Texas. His relative says neither of them were alerted to any plans to transfer him, or a reason for it.

The DHS did not specify why Cora Pérez was transferred, adding that ICE makes custody determinations on a “case-by-case” basis based on “various factors”.

The revelations come as ICE’s detention practices continue to come under fire amid allegations of mistreatment, and as an increasing number of sporadic hunger strikes have been breaking out in ICE facilities across the country.

The two men’s cases in Texas, revealed here for the first time, are some of the most recent instances of government lawyers seeking a federal judge’s permission, as required by ICE policy, and receiving the go-ahead to force-feed detained hunger strikers. The Guardian’s reporting is based on court records, interviews, dozens of messages exchanged and an interview conducted with Cora Pérez via a facility phone. It further reveals how the Trump administration is increasingly obtaining such court orders to force-feed detained immigrants, a secretive practice widely condemned as torture by human rights organizations and medical ethics groups.

Detainees driven to hunger strike are typically using it as a last resort to protest against poor conditions and the Trump administration’s preference for arrest and prolonged detention while their civil immigration cases proceed through the system.

Cora Pérez said detention center staff inserted the feeding tube and left it in his body, a not uncommon practice, according to experts, and introduced nutrition – first a “clear liquid”, followed by a “milky liquid”, he recalled – through the tube twice more that day, before he cracked and said he broke his hunger strike, citing what he called “horrific torture”. He began voluntarily drinking nutritional shakes the following day, he said.

“ICE does not hold back on anything, and they do anything they want, like we have seen, even killing their own US citizens,” he wrote to the Guardian, referring to the fatal shootings of Renee Good by an ICE officer and Alex Pretti by a border patrol officer in January of this year during Trump’s pivotal immigration crackdown on Minneapolis.

Detained hunger strikers subjected to involuntary medical procedures, including force-feeding, have rarely spoken out about their cases or revealed their identities, much less while still detained. Cora Pérez’s messages offer a rare glimpse at conditions inside a detention center’s restricted medical unit where hunger strikers and suicidal detainees are held.

“They just took \[the Uzbek man\] in an ambulance after \[him\] fainting in front of the medical lobby where they take our vitals, our weight and our temperature,” Cora Pérez said in an alarmed message last Monday morning.

The Uzbek man was returned the following day to the facility, Cora Pérez said.

“I see him every day because I see him in the room in front of me, but they don’t let us talk to each other,” he added.

The Guardian independently confirmed the Uzbek’s man identity but is not publicly naming him, because efforts to contact him have been unsuccessful. The man arrived at the Mexico-US border in April 2022 and was released into the country while navigating his immigration case. He was arrested by border patrol officials in April of this year and placed in detention. The man does not appear to have any criminal record and the DHS did not point to any criminal history.

In a statement, DHS said that after they received the court’s permission to force-feed the Uzbek man, he “has voluntarily taken in fluids and there has been NO force-feeding or forced hydration”.

Security operations at the sprawling Port Isabel facility in Los Fresnos, Texas, are run by a private prison company, Akima Global Services, while healthcare is primarily handled by government workers.

“ICE respects detainees’ rights to exercise self-expression and medical autonomy by refusing nourishment and medical care,” the DHS said in a statement. “ICE Health Services Corps may provide involuntary medical treatment only to prevent imminent life-threatening harm or death. Medical staff may provide treatment only to medically stabilize the patient, bringing the detainee outside the imminent harm, incapacitation, or death.”

The US attorney’s office in the southern district of Texas, which represented ICE in its force-feeding request, did not respond to multiple requests for comment. Virginia-headquartered Akima Global Services, and its parent company Nana Regional Corporation, based in Alaska, did not respond to a request for comment.

Force-feeding cases are shrouded in secrecy. After a detainee launches a hunger strike, ICE often sequesters them in medical isolation cells for monitoring, according to ICE’s detention standards. The DHS said that ICE continues to offer hunger strikers three meals per day.

After a certain period of not eating, which varies per case, ICE will request a federal judge’s permission to force-feed the hunger striker. Many court records, and sometimes entire court dockets, are sealed and hidden from public view. In Cora Pérez and the Uzbek man’s cases, like in others, they did not have any legal representation to challenge the force-feeding requests.

The Guardian found at least five instances in which ICE requested permission to force-feed hunger strikers in Port Isabel since January 2025. The federal judge who ruled on Cora Perez and the Uzbek man, Rolando Olvera, has similarly ordered in at least three other cases, records show. Olvera’s judicial assistant said the court had no comment for this article.

ICE is known to have requested permission to force-feed at least 21 detainees across the US since January 2025, the Guardian found, but the number is probably higher since an unknown number of records and dockets remain sealed, unsearchable and not feasible to locate. Most of the cases coinciding with the second Trump administration and tracked by the Guardian are in Texas and Florida, with others in Georgia, Arizona and Washington state. Under the Biden administration, ICE force-feeding requests were also made in Louisiana and California.

Amy Zeidan, an emergency medicine physician based in Atlanta and an expert on healthcare in immigration detention, said force-feeding hunger strikers can amount to “torture”, and lead to significant psychological distress. She also said it was a violation of medical ethics.

“Essentially it’s like inserting a straw into your nose,” Zeidan said. “You have a gag reflex, so most times people will gag, and that’s really uncomfortable. And people will even vomit repeatedly if it continues to irritate their gag reflex.”

Zeidan added that the forceful insertion of a feeding tube can lead to the swelling of the nostrils and the throat, and even tear them, leading to bleeding.

“It is like torture – somebody is doing a painful procedure to you that you don’t consent to,” Zeidan added. “Autonomy is a fundamental principle of medical ethics. We can’t do something to patients if they don’t want to, even if we think it’s good for them.”

There are numerous cells and rooms inside the Port Isabel medical unit, including isolation cells and shared rooms for ill detainees, according to Cora Pérez. In recent weeks, there were five people in the Port Isabel medical isolation cells used for hunger striking or suicidal detainees, he added. He described the cells as “practically freezing”, constantly surveilled with a security camera, and with just a bed, toilet and sink. As well as himself, he says he observed the Uzbek man, a Middle Eastern man, a “tall” eastern European man and a Black man of unknown nationality in the isolation cells. Unit detainees are escorted by facility staff to showers and sometimes receive yard and television access, he said.

Cora Pérez worries for the other detainees. The Black man, whose identity or nationality he does not know, seems to have “serious mental health problems”, Cora Pérez observed.

“He harms himself and spends the night yelling and hitting the door, and does not let anyone sleep,” he said.

The Guardian has independently confirmed the eastern European and Middle Eastern men’s identities, but is not publicly naming them because efforts to contact them have been unsuccessful. The DHS did not comment on the other men inside the medical isolation unit, saying they could not comment without the Guardian providing their identities.

Cora Pérez had left his son and parents in Cuba and requested asylum at the Mexico-US border in 2023, according to a relative who spoke to the Guardian on condition of anonymity due to fear of retaliation by immigration authorities. Cora Pérez went to live with the relative in Florida, where he worked in maintenance at a hotel and as a food delivery worker, he said.

In March 2025, Cora Pérez was arrested by local police and later convicted of two misdemeanors, including “breach of peace” and “obstructing an officer without violence”, according to local records. He was sentenced to two months in jail, his relative said. But ICE placed a hold on him and as he was being released in June 2025, immigration officials took him into custody – a common system – and soon transferred him to the Adelanto detention center, a privately-run facility in California.

Days in Adelanto turned to weeks, then months, then over a year, according to a federal court order denying one of his petitions requesting his release. His multiple requests to immigration and ordinary federal courts for release from detention, while he fights his asylum case, have been unsuccessful.

“All his claims will be heard by an immigration judge, and he will receive due process. This administration will not ignore the rule of law,” DHS said. “Criminal illegal aliens are not welcome in the US.”

In August, he stopped eating to protest against his protracted detention.

“I have spent two birthdays behind ICE’s bars,” he wrote. “The reasons I did the hunger strike in Adelanto are for my political asylum, for the time I have spent detained, \[and\] because I have a 14-year-old son who is starving to death in Cuba because he does not have my help.

“Also due to the mistreatment by the officials,” he added.

Cora Pérez did not tell his family about the hunger strike, so as not to further worry them. It was not until he was transferred to Port Isabel in late September that he confessed to his relative he had been on a prolonged hunger strike.

“He doesn’t share details so that I won’t get upset or worry,” the relative said in a phone interview.

Cora Pérez’s mother, who is in Cuba, “does not know anything, because she is sick, and with his detention she has gotten worse”, the relative added, between tears. “I don’t want her nor his grandmother to know anything about it,” the relative added.

On 30 October, the federal prosecutors requested permission for ICE to forcibly feed and hydrate Cora Pérez. Hours later, a federal judge approved the procedures without hearing from Cora Pérez. Cora Pérez told the Guardian in various instances he felt it was unfair he was not given the opportunity to present his case to the judge before the judge approved his force-feeding.

“It’s very disturbing because the judge is basically making a decision on information that is only provided by one side,” said Linus Chan, a professor of clinical law and the director of the detainee rights clinic at the University of Minnesota law school. “That just seems ridiculous.”

Cora Pérez was force-fed the following day, he said in his messages and in a phone call, adding that he did not physically resist because he “had seen a lot of mistreatment of others detained”.

“\[ICE does\] what they want with us, whatever they want, because a federal judge gave them permission,” he added. “I have suffered on the island \[of Cuba\] and now at the hands of ICE.”

After asking Cora Pérez about the DHS’s denials that he was force-fed, he repeated that he was. “Brother, ICE says and does whatever they want. They deny, punish, retaliate and do everything at their own will. They have even sent Cubans to Africa,” he said.

The number of people detained by ICE has soared under the Trump administration. And due to policy and legal changes, tens of thousands of people are forced to stay in detention for long periods while they fight their immigration cases.

Chan, from the University of Minnesota, says prolonged detention and delays in their cases lead to logical conclusion. “That’s exactly when people protest,” he said.

“And the only form of protest, for many of these people, is a hunger strike,” he said.

As Trump’s hardline immigration crackdown continues and people are detained as a first resort while their cases play out, Chan said: “Hunger strikes will become more common.”

articles.title: The Case for A.I. Optimism
articles.author: David Remnick
articles.body_markdown:
In Washington, it is essential to read, or at least display, the collected works of Robert Caro. (The spines of “The Power Broker” and the multivolume biography in progress of Lyndon Johnson are compulsory in every Zoom background on cable news.) In Silicon Valley, the required reading list surely includes Richard Rhodes’s “The Making of the Atomic Bomb,” a magisterial history of the discovery of nuclear fission and its epochal resolution with the Manhattan Project and the start of the nuclear age. Not a few of the tech barons and innovators of our time see themselves as neo-Oppenheimers. When A.I. reaches maturity, it may get its Caro or Rhodes. In the meantime, Kevin Roose’s lucid journalistic account “The AGI Chronicles: The Inside Story of the Race to Create an Artificial Superintelligence” does the trick.

Roose is a classic beat reporter, having covered technology for outlets including the *Times, The Atlantic*, *New York*, and NPR. Recently, he bolted from the *Times* to work independently, and, these days, he is co-hosting a podcast, with Casey Newton, called “Machine Gods.” Among the most interesting A.I. podcasters around—on “Dwarkesh Podcast,” “No Priors,” and “Latent Space,” to name a few—Roose stands out for his ability to tell a story with narrative drive. He breaks things down neatly and clearly for the non-expert.

I spoke with Roose for The New Yorker Radio Hour just before Anthropic, Dario Amodei’s A.I. outfit, made what has turned out to be the largest initial public offering of all time. And, of course, while Amodei and his colleagues were coming into their many billions, Jensen Huang, the former king of the Nvidia empire, which has by many metrics powered the A.I. revolution, was appealing to his old board of directors to let him back in after his humbling. On the utopian-to-doomer scale, Roose is . . . hopeful. Or, as they say on the Sabbath Gasbag shows, cautiously optimistic. His interlocutor, by nature, is less so. We had a lot to talk about.

**Anthropic is just going public. In their filing paperwork for the first half of 2026, they reported a revenue of $16.3 billion and a net loss of $80.7 billion. The company is also on the hook for $900 billion in future obligations for chips and data-center leases. How do they make the math make sense?**

Basically, the bet that investors are making on Anthropic is that it will continue to grow at something close to the rate that it has been growing for the last several years. This is a company that has been growing faster than any company at its scale in the history of capitalism. Four or five years ago, they had essentially no revenue. Three years ago, they had tens of millions in revenue, and it’s been growing tenfold every year for the last three or four years. Not ten per cent; ten times.

That is due, in large part, to the popularity of their models for coding and other white-collar work. And the bet is that this growth just continues—that as these tools get better and more helpful, that more white-collar knowledge workers will incorporate them into their work, and developers will be paying much more, because usage will continue to go up.

The math *doesn’t* make sense if you think that A.I. is already as popular and widely adopted as it will ever be. It starts to make more sense if you anticipate that what has been happening for the past few years will keep happening—which is that the models get better and more people use them.

Some companies out here in Silicon Valley are already spending more on A.I. tokens than they are on payroll. So the long-term bet is that the economy essentially switches over from running primarily on human labor and paying human salaries to running on A.I. labor and paying token prices.

**If that in fact is the right bet to make, give me a picture of the economy on an A.I. basis, as opposed to human labor. What’s it going to look like?**

I think it looks a lot like my company. I’m starting a startup, Machine Gods Media. We are a six-person company right now. In our Slack, where we communicate all day, we have six humans and probably a dozen agents. And the agents are doing things we don’t know how to do ourselves. They’re writing code. I just got back from what I jokingly call our engineering department, but it’s really just a bunch of Claudes running around. They’re building tools, helping with scheduling and coördination, with all of the pieces that go into making podcasts, aside from the actual talking into a microphone.

**What would those be? Is it so complex that you need Claude to do it?**

It turns out to be pretty complex. For example, we have all these deliverables. When you have a show, it needs to get delivered in all these different formats. Apple needs one format, Spotify needs one format, and YouTube needs another format. And it’s all got captions, and titles, and descriptions, and metadata. And all that used to have to be done by hand. Now we have this tool that does it all for us.

**Tell me how that works for a big law firm, as opposed to a six-person podcasting outfit.**

It might not be a big law firm. It might actually be a small law firm, in terms of the human payroll and footprint. It might be a law firm that only has ten people, but, using A.I., they have access to essentially unlimited amounts of paralegal, junior-associate-quality labor. And so they can do, with ten people, what a more traditional firm might need a thousand people for. That may or may not be possible—there might be gaps in what these models do that might make them unsuited to that level of integration. But that’s the bet that investors are making. It’s not just that Anthropic will continue to grow or that its models will get better, but that A.I. will become the foundation of a new kind of company that will be built on top of A.I.

**How many of these companies can prevail in the new world of A.I.? We have Anthropic and OpenAI, among others. Who’s in the lead and why?**

Right now there are two clear frontier labs: OpenAI and Anthropic. I would say that, of the two, Anthropic may be slightly ahead; its models are considered better by some metrics. But those two are definitely the front-runners. Then there’s a small-to-medium drop-off before Google DeepMind, which to my mind is the third frontier lab. **The P.R. that I get is that Anthropic is the good company, as you suggest. The job interviews even have a moral dimension. Whereas OpenAI is quite a different thing. Is that fair?**

As someone once told me, his superpower is being able to zero in on exactly what you want to hear and give it to you. Dario is very high-I.Q., stubborn, and neurotic. He’s a moral absolutist, with a strong belief in what is good and right and righteous. He’s also a brilliant scientist who foresaw many of today’s A.I. trends and dynamics years before anyone else. His superpower—and his kryptonite—is that he cannot lie. Sometimes it leads to him standing his ground and standing up for his principles. When the Pentagon says, “We want to use Claude for whatever we want to do,” he’s the guy who has the cojones to stand up to them, while everyone else is busy trying to snivel and get on their good side.

Yes. And a lot of people at Anthropic saw that and admired Dario for standing his ground, even when it would have been expedient for him to say whatever it took to make Pete Hegseth happy. But it also leads to these incredible moments. Remember that press briefing outside the White House, where all these A.I. C.E.O.s were standing in a semicircle? **Really?**

Almost everyone likes the human-written one.

A decade is so long from now, David.

**That’s fair.**

I struggle to think about what the world will look like in a year.

**Really?**

I do. I think parts of it will look largely the same. I will still probably drop my kid off at school, go to the grocery store. There will be parts of my life that are much the same.

**But when you and I talk next Thanksgiving, what will we have experienced? What changes will have been brought into our lives over the course of a year?**

If the next year plays out in a way that is thoughtful, I think we will have put in place vastly more guardrails.

**Where do you get your confidence that thoughtfulness is anywhere in abundance in the U.S. government, or anywhere else?**

Thoughtful, or maybe just self-interested. I think we have a deep desire to remain in control of our society, of our government, of our surroundings, of our lives. We still want to be in the driver’s seat. And as long as we recognize that A.I. is not just a tool or a hype bubble but is actually, in some sense, a type of entity that could displace us at the top of the intelligence ladder . . . We could be the second-smartest thing on earth a year from now, and I think we have a lot to do between now and then. But my hope would be that we look back and say, “Wow, that was a crazy year, and a bunch of cybersecurity incidents happened, and we fixed a bunch of stuff just in time, and it was like Y2K. It could have been this major crisis, but we averted it through heroic effort and late nights at the computer terminal.” That, I think, is the good outcome.

**That’s a lot of close calls to endure and still be an optimist.**

We’ve done it before.

**When?**

Y2K, the Cold War. The Industrial Revolution played out over seventy-five or eighty years, but we muddled through. It did not lead to human extinction.

**A lot of people talk about a kill switch for A.I., as if, when things get out of hand, suddenly somebody goes to a special room and turns a switch and A.I. is turned off and things can settle down, and whatever is broken can be fixed. What is a kill switch? Is it an imaginary construct or is it a real thing?**

It’s an imaginary construct. I think it comes from science-fiction movies or thrillers where—

**That’s where I get all my best stuff.**

The red lights in the control room start blinking, and the engineer sprints over to the server rack and yanks out the cord—

**Clips the blue wire instead of the red wire. Bruce Willis always chooses correctly.**

Unfortunately, that is not how modern A.I. systems are running. They are distributed across huge numbers of servers and data centers. And there’s been some research into how these things can actually replicate themselves on smart devices, like smart ovens and toasters in your home. We can’t just pull the plug if it might mean taking down some huge chunk of computers across the world.

**In a few years, are we going to be at twenty-five-per-cent unemployment?**

I hope not. I hope we will continue to find useful and valuable things to do, but I think a lot of that depends on the decisions we make not just as a public sector, as the government, as regulators, but as employers and business leaders. I mean, do you fire your human workers as soon as they’re no longer technically adding anything to the organization, or do you retrain them for some other part of the job? I hope that we have enlightened leaders out there who will see it as part of their responsibility not to conduct layoffs as soon as it’s technically feasible.

**Where does your sense of confidence, whether in the government or the private sector, reside?**

My confidence resides in the public, actually. As recipients, users, and, in some cases, victims of this technology, we are not powerless or impotent. We have seen large, society-altering technological transformations turn out great, because people made it turn out great. My optimism also comes from the general belief that technology usually makes our lives better in the long run. ♦

Sam Altman is a master salesman and fund-raiser. That is his superpower. He ran Y Combinator, the startup incubator, before leaving to become the C.E.O. of OpenAI. His reputation is that of an extremely ambitious, high-E.Q. people pleaser. As someone once told me, his superpower is being able to zero in on exactly what you want to hear and give it to you. That has served him well in some instances and poorly in others, such as when his board decided that he was lying to them and tried to fire him. It has also contributed to his reputation as somewhat two-faced or duplicitous.
**What about Dario?**

Dario is very high-I.Q., stubborn, and neurotic. He’s a moral absolutist, with a strong belief in what is good and right and righteous. He’s also a brilliant scientist who foresaw many of today’s A.I. trends and dynamics years before anyone else. His superpower—and his kryptonite—is that he cannot lie. Someone close to him once told me, “Dario is a guy who cannot tell a lie to save his life, which is an asset for us on even-numbered days and a liability on odd-numbered days.”
**How does that work?**

Sometimes it leads to him standing his ground and standing up for his principles. When the Pentagon says, “We want to use Claude for whatever we want to do,” he’s the guy who has the cojones to stand up to them, while everyone else is busy trying to snivel and get on their good side.
**The Pentagon banned the use of Claude.**

Yes. And a lot of people at Anthropic saw that and admired Dario for standing his ground, even when it would have been expedient for him to say whatever it took to make Pete Hegseth happy. But it also leads to these incredible moments. Remember that press briefing outside the White House, where all these A.I. C.E.O.s were standing in a semicircle? Dario was practically jumping out of his skin, unable to conceal his displeasure at having to stand alongside these cowards. He couldn’t hide it. It was written all over his face. So, I think that’s what they meant by an asset on even-numbered days and a liability on odd-numbered days.
**What has stood out most for you in Anthropic’s I.P.O. and the way this has all gone?**
I think about the absolute rocket-ship trajectory this company has been on, more than any other company I’ve ever covered, and perhaps more than any company that has ever existed.

The first time I visited Anthropic to report on them was three years ago. Three years—not that long ago. They had a hundred and fifty employees, working out of a cramped office in Jackson Square, in San Francisco. They didn’t even have a sign-in desk. You just took the elevator up and started walking around. They had no plans to make money. They weren’t a commercial enterprise and had barely released a product. They were a bunch of A.I.-safety-obsessed nerds who seemed genuinely worried about the technology.

If you had told me on that first visit that, three years later, this company would go public at a valuation of more than a trillion dollars and become one of the largest companies in the world, I would have laughed in your face. It seemed so unlikely that they would go from a little hundred-and-fifty-person startup to a company with, I think, more than five thousand employees, and one of the biggest in the world.

**There’s perhaps a too easy confidence in the world of long-form journalism that what we do is special—that gathering information, analyzing it, and presenting it in narrative form is something A.I. simply won’t be able to do. Whereas asking for the ten best restaurants in Seattle is easy enough: you can scrape that information off the internet and present it. Are we living in a dream?**

I think we are. I think there will still be a market for human-authored work—there’s just something about A.I. writing that is hollow and generic. But what’s interesting is that researchers have conducted blind tests in which people are shown two snippets of writing and asked which they prefer. Most of the time, when they don’t know which is which, people prefer the A.I.-generated work.
**Really?**
But when people learn which one was A.I. and which one was human-written, the preference swaps.
**So, what does that tell you?**
Almost everyone likes the human-written one.
**They like the *idea* of the human-written one, but they might not innately like the human one at all.**
I think the future of at least some writing will involve humans sticking their names on A.I.-generated literature because they don’t want to break that connection, that spell, with the audience.
**That is not entirely reassuring, Kevin.**
I’m sorry. I wish I had a rosier view.

**On the continuum from doomers, people who believe A.I. will kill us all, to those who are absolutely sanguine about this whole thing—who think it’s going to be great and we’re going to work one day a week and spend the rest of our time sunning ourselves and, I don’t know, whistling—you are pretty sanguine about this subject, and the opposite of a doomer. Am I right?**
I am an optimist by temperament. I believe that we can and should thread this needle, but we’ve got a lot of work to do.
**What concerns you the most?**

Right now, what concerns me is an intelligence explosion. That’s a term in the A.I. industry for what could happen after A.I. becomes capable of building A.I. It’s sometimes called “recursive self-improvement.” It’s the idea that an A.I. model becomes superhuman at developing other A.I. models, capable of doing the entire workload of a senior research engineer at OpenAI or Anthropic. That hasn’t happened yet, but some people, including at *METR*, a credible third-party organization, believe it could happen within the next year. At that point, you could use A.I., in a closed, no-human environment, to train more capable A.I. models.
**What are the potential disasters, in concrete terms, that could come out of that manifestation?**

If these people are right—and let’s caveat that they might not be—but if we were to see, say, a decade’s worth of improvements in A.I. capabilities compressed into a single year, because all of this could happen at machine speed rather than at human speed, I think we’d be looking at systems that start breaking a lot of things all at once. We’re already seeing some of this with cyberattacks, the incident involving Hugging Face, and the U.S. government scrambling to contain threats to critical infrastructure from these A.I. models. Imagine that, but times ten or times a hundred. There’s just a base rate of chaos and instability—
**And, at the same time, a very low propensity toward regulation.**
For now. But I think that could change very quickly. In fact, I believe part of the reason the Democrats won the midterms so decisively was—
**Anxiety about A.I.**

People had anxiety about A.I. So things could change pretty quickly on this. As unpopular as A.I. might be right now, I expect it to be even more unpopular. Right now we’re seeing this massive backlash against A.I. Unemployment is still under five per cent. It was not at all intuitive to me that we would see this level of backlash before any of the widespread job losses arrived.
**Well, because you’re reading about it every two seconds, and you’re seeing reports on it on television and YouTube. There’s an anticipatory anxiety about it.**

But think about how much more anxiety there would be if people were actually losing their jobs en masse. I desperately want that not to happen, but, to me, the timing of this backlash has been a little surprising, because it seems like there’s still a lot more risk out there to be priced in.

**Now, I think you have to be impressed that we’ve gotten this far in our conversation without having mentioned Jensen Huang. What do you make of this? What did we just see? My God, it’s like the worst James Bond plot you have ever experienced.**
It really is. It’s dime-store stuff. This is a guy who has been so central to the A.I. boom. Nvidia’s G.P.U.s are the reason we have any of this today.
**Tell us what a G.P.U. is.**

G.P.U. is a graphics-processing unit. Basically, a modern A.I. chip is descended from these things that gamers used to stick in their PCs to render backgrounds and polygons better. And Jensen Huang is the reason that those chips are now the most valuable commodity in the world—so valued that we’ve had to pass special export controls to prevent China from getting access to them, because, if compute is the determining factor between success and failure, we don’t want them to get our most powerful chips.
**Do you figure they have it anyway?**
It sure seems like they’ve gotten a bunch of them anyway. And the question is—
**Thanks to Alice Huang?**

Well, there’s this whole gray market of cutouts in Malaysia, Singapore, and other countries. They’ll buy a bunch of Nvidia chips because they’re allowed to buy them—they’re not China—and then they’ll either set up a data center and give Chinese companies remote access to it, or, in some cases, they’ll just smuggle the chips into China. And one of the major questions going forward is how much of this Jensen Huang knew about. Was he aware that Nvidia chips were being smuggled into China? And how much did his relationship with Alice Huang and Megaspeed factor into that?
**So, what are the ramifications of this?**
I mean, we’ll see where Jensen Huang ends up. He’s now saying he would like to return to Nvidia. I suspect that won’t work.
**I’d like to win the Super Bowl, too, but I don’t think that’s happening.**

In the short term, it means that the entire industry will have to approach things slightly differently. For many years, Jensen Huang has been the sole guy with control of the commodity that everyone in A.I. needs—the key ingredient. His relationships really determined who got how many of Nvidia’s latest chips. It was not a pure auction market. It was, like, “Oh, Alice Huang and I are friends, so I’ll save some of these chips for Megaspeed.” Or, “Elon Musk and I go way back. I’ll give him a big allotment.”
**Who benefitted most from the relationship?**

Elon Musk has gotten a very large allotment of chips that was maybe out of step with his company’s importance in A.I. because he and Jensen Huang are old friends. I think Sam Altman has benefitted from a close relationship with Jensen Huang.

Dario Amodei and Anthropic have actually not had a close relationship with Jensen Huang. As I reported in my book, there was a very tense meeting between Dario Amodei and Jensen Huang—it was the first time they’d met, and Jensen was basically grandstanding about how big the data center they were going to build was, while Dario was peppering him with somewhat rude questions. “Oh, how big is it going to be? What order of magnitude? Where are you going to get the power?” And eventually Dario mutters to someone sitting next to him that Jensen is acting Trump-like, and the two of them didn’t like each other for a long time.
**If Dario didn’t have that kind of access for Anthropic, how has he prevailed anyway?**

They have adopted a very unusual compute strategy—they have essentially gotten a little bit from everyone. They have a bunch of Amazon chips called Trainium. They rent a bunch of chips from Google, and they have a bunch of Nvidia chips, too. Rather than tethering themselves to one chip company or one hyperscaler, they have drawn from all of them to varying degrees. But they’re compute-constrained just like everyone else in the industry. They wish they had more data centers. They wish they had more chips. No one’s got enough.

**I think it’s fair to say that when the internet and the iPhone first appeared we had no real concept of what an unregulated experiment on human consciousness and behavior these things would represent, on all kinds of levels—whether it was about reading, concentration, mental health, or how we related to each other. Here we are again, on the brink of another revolution that is arguably much greater—something vastly more complicated. Despite your optimism, in terms of human relations and the way we live our lives, what are you expecting in the next decade or so?**
A decade is so long from now, David.
**That’s fair.**
I struggle to think about what the world will look like in a year.
**Really?**
I do. I think parts of it will look largely the same. I will still probably drop my kid off at school, go to the grocery store. There will be parts of my life that are much the same.
**But when you and I talk next Thanksgiving, what will we have experienced? What changes will have been brought into our lives over the course of a year?**
If the next year plays out in a way that is thoughtful, I think we will have put in place vastly more guardrails.
**Where do you get your confidence that thoughtfulness is anywhere in abundance in the U.S. government, or anywhere else?**

Thoughtful, or maybe just self-interested. I think we have a deep desire to remain in control of our society, of our government, of our surroundings, of our lives. We still want to be in the driver’s seat. And as long as we recognize that A.I. is not just a tool or a hype bubble but is actually, in some sense, a type of entity that could displace us at the top of the intelligence ladder . . . We could be the second-smartest thing on earth a year from now, and I think we have a lot to do between now and then. But my hope would be that we look back and say, “Wow, that was a crazy year, and a bunch of cybersecurity incidents happened, and we fixed a bunch of stuff just in time, and it was like Y2K. It could have been this major crisis, but we averted it through heroic effort and late nights at the computer terminal.” That, I think, is the good outcome.
**That’s a lot of close calls to endure and still be an optimist.**
We’ve done it before.
**When?**
Y2K, the Cold War. The Industrial Revolution played out over seventy-five or eighty years, but we muddled through. It did not lead to human extinction.

**A lot of people talk about a kill switch for A.I., as if, when things get out of hand, suddenly somebody goes to a special room and turns a switch and A.I. is turned off and things can settle down, and whatever is broken can be fixed. What is a kill switch? Is it an imaginary construct or is it a real thing?**
It’s an imaginary construct. I think it comes from science-fiction movies or thrillers where—
**That’s where I get all my best stuff.**
The red lights in the control room start blinking, and the engineer sprints over to the server rack and yanks out the cord—
**Clips the blue wire instead of the red wire. Bruce Willis always chooses correctly.**

Unfortunately, that is not how modern A.I. systems are running. They are distributed across huge numbers of servers and data centers. And there’s been some research into how these things can actually replicate themselves on smart devices, like smart ovens and toasters in your home. We can’t just pull the plug if it might mean taking down some huge chunk of computers across the world.
**In a few years, are we going to be at twenty-five-per-cent unemployment?**

I hope not. I hope we will continue to find useful and valuable things to do, but I think a lot of that depends on the decisions we make not just as a public sector, as the government, as regulators, but as employers and business leaders. I mean, do you fire your human workers as soon as they’re no longer technically adding anything to the organization, or do you retrain them for some other part of the job? I hope that we have enlightened leaders out there who will see it as part of their responsibility not to conduct layoffs as soon as it’s technically feasible.
**Where does your sense of confidence, whether in the government or the private sector, reside?**

My confidence resides in the public, actually. As recipients, users, and, in some cases, victims of this technology, we are not powerless or impotent. We have seen large, society-altering technological transformations turn out great, because people made it turn out great. My optimism also comes from the general belief that technology usually makes our lives better in the long run. ♦

articles.title: The race to understand why young people are dying from colon cancer
articles.author: Lauren J Young
articles.body_markdown:
In 2022 Reuben Cheatem thought he had food poisoning—again. The painter and visual artist had first spotted blood in his stool the year before, and he assumed it was from repeated episodes of bad food poisoning. But this time the digestive issues, stomach pains and irregular bowel movements wouldn’t let up. After three weeks, he knew they weren’t the result of contaminated food or an everyday bug. His doctor thought he had diverticulitis, a type of colon inflammation, and prescribed antibiotics and pain medications. After a few months, the symptoms returned. Nothing worked. On “about my fourth trip to the ER and my fourth CT \[computed tomography\] scan, a specialist said there was no way that \[this\] was diverticulitis,” Cheatem says. “It was something further.”

Doctors found an advanced malignant tumor in Cheatem’s lower colon. That September, at age 42, he was diagnosed with stage III colorectal cancer, which set him on a path to surgery and chemotherapy.

He was completely thrown by the words coming out of the doctor’s mouth. Cheatem thought he was healthy; he ate healthily and exercised regularly, and in his artwork he even avoided using oil-based paints known to contain carcinogens. Plus, he had no family history of colorectal cancer. “The cancer diagnosis itself came as a shock because I felt like I had been taking so many steps to simply not get cancer,” says Cheatem, who now lives in Texas.

Stories like Cheatem’s are becoming more common as severe colorectal cancer rates rise among younger, traditionally low-risk people. And these cases have grown increasingly visible. Actors James Van Der Beek and Chadwick Boseman were both in their 40s when they died from the disease. The uptick in cases has some scientists wondering whether they’re dealing with an entirely new type of colorectal cancer. As they race to find clues to explain the disturbing trend, several theories are emerging.

Colorectal cancer is still far more common in adults older than age 65. What’s shifted is the frequency of cases: the rate among older adults has been declining, but the number of diagnoses in younger people has continued to escalate since the mid-1990s. In response to the trend, in 2021, the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) lowered the recommended screening age from 50 to 45. In January 2026, the American Cancer Society’s annual report stated that colorectal cancer had officially become the deadliest cancer in people under age 50 in the U.S. Similar increases in rates of the cancer in younger age groups have been seen globally. People born in the 1990s have at least a fourfold-higher risk of developing colorectal cancer than those born in the 1960s in countries such as Australia, Canada and England. Health registries in Korea, Japan, Thailand and India have also reported increasing cases over the past several decades. Epidemiologists have noticed that the spike in incidence is tied to the time when a person was born, pointing toward generational shifts in risk or exposure.

“Is this a completely new cancer that we’re now seeing in young people for whatever reason?” —Andrea Cercek *Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center*

Most experts agree that the cause or causes won’t be clear-cut. Family history and genetics have been strongly associated with higher risk. But Kimmie Ng, an oncologist and leader in early-onset colorectal cancer research, and her team at the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute have seen not only an overall surge in cases in young people but more advanced-stage tumors in people who have no family history of cancer and are otherwise in good health, similar to Cheatem. Some research suggests that generational shifts in lifestyle, such as eating more processed foods and getting less physical activity, and environmental factors—including exposure to plastics and toxic chemicals—probably play some role.

Unknown exposures in childhood or even in the womb could be factors, Ng says. Delays in getting tested may also explain part of it, she adds. A 2018 report found that 67 percent of people diagnosed with early-onset colorectal cancer went to at least two physicians before receiving that diagnosis. Ng suspects, however, that there is more to the mysterious trend. “Regardless of how they were diagnosed, the survival of the very youngest patients is still worse,” she says. “That suggests to me that there may be something biologically different.”

Johns Hopkins University oncologist Elizabeth Jaffee agrees that delays in diagnosis go only so far toward explaining the surge. “We don’t know what’s driving these \[tumors\] biologically yet, and that’s really the problem,” she says. “We need more biology to go along with all of this epidemiology and correlative studies.”

Every year, leading cancer experts flock to one of the biggest meetings in their field—the American Association of Cancer Research’s annual meeting. And increasingly, the phenomenon of early-onset colorectal cancer is a major topic of conversation. At the 2025 conference, Jaffee moderated a panel focused on the challenges facing colorectal cancer researchers and patients. Panelist and oncologist Andrea Cercek posed a query that has continued to weigh heavily on researchers and clinicians.

“Is this a completely new cancer that we’re now seeing in young people for whatever reason?” asked Cercek, co-director of the Center for Young Onset Colorectal and Gastrointestinal Cancer at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center. “Or \[has there\] just been this shift that’s now happening younger and younger?”

Cancer can be a slow, surreptitious illness—for decades researchers have called it a “disease of the aging.” Cells constantly turn over, and little mistakes—or mutations—can sneak into new batches. The body usually catches and eliminates these faulty cells, but with age, that process can slow down, and abnormal cells can pile up. “Mutation after mutation happens, and then it turns into a carcinoma,” Cercek told me.

Colorectal cancer typically follows a 10- to 15-year timeline from normal cell to small growth or polyp to, eventually, a larger mass or tumor. If mutant cells are not detected, they may amass over decades in older adults. Cercek and other researchers are investigating whether something might accelerate the timeline in people who develop the disease at a younger age.

Genetically, colorectal tumors look surprisingly similar in young and old bodies, involving roughly the same groups of mutations. In 2021 Cercek’s team found that tumors from people as young as age 14 and as old as age 93 showed no significant genetic differences. But how those mutations occur in the first place could explain why the tumors pop up earlier in some people.

“Babies or young kids or adolescents \[could be\] exposed to something in the environment that leads to some biological changes early in life that then predispose them to the development of cancer at a younger age than we have historically seen,” says Ng, who leads the Young-Onset Colorectal Cancer Center at Dana-Farber. “I do think that it is key to try to study early-life factors, though it’s really hard to do.”

Ng helped to create the center in 2019 to address the trend head-on, launching research that has involved collecting various samples, including blood, stool and tumor tissue, from patients under age 50 treated at Dana-Farber. The data gathered over time might reveal links between tumor mutations and the gut microbiome.

A different team solidified an important lead in 2025: in data collected from 11 countries on four continents, the researchers identified two peculiar patterns of DNA, or mutational signatures, whose prevalence was more than three times higher among people under age 40 with colorectal cancer than among people age 70 and older who also had the disease. These mutational signatures can tell doctors what jump-started the chain of events that led to the cancerous tumor.

The researchers suggest that the two mutational signatures are linked to a toxin called colibactin, which is produced by gut bacteria such as *Escherichia coli* that contain genes encoding polyketide synthase enzymes, called *pks*-positive bacteria. The toxin might damage DNA in healthy colon crypts—tubelike mucus glands that line the colon and rectum—potentially prompting tumor growth.

“Modeling investigations seem to find that \[*pks*-positive *E. coli*\] colonize very, very young individuals, probably in the first decade of life,” says Ng, who was not involved in the study.\* “One of the hypotheses is that perhaps \[some\] young children are colonized with *pks*-positive *E. coli*.” Past evidence has found high levels of *pks-positive E. coli in infants* without any associated negative health effects or higher risk of cancer. But Ng says further research studies are needed to determine the extent of *pks*-positive bacteria in children and the possible effects on health outcomes.

A group of researchers, including Ng’s team, plans to confirm these findings in a larger population in the U.S. and elsewhere. The scientists are also aiming to better understand the prevalence of *pks*-positive *E. coli* in children.

When Ng looks through her microscope at young patients’ tissue samples, she tries to coax stories out of the tumors—little signs of their progression and characteristics. Are there certain molecular traits that make some tumors spread faster or more aggressively than others?

For instance, Ng’s and Cercek’s teams have independently found that people who are younger than age 35 when they’re diagnosed with colon cancer tend to die more quickly than any other age group. People in their 20s and 30s, groups where the rates are rising most steeply, have the worst survival outcomes—even compared with patients in their 60s, Ng says.

Under the microscope, younger individuals’ tumor cells can appear more disorganized and abnormal compared with healthy tissue, Ng explains. Past research has shown that early-onset colorectal cancers in patients under age 40 also have higher rates of signet ring cell carcinoma—a type of cancer that is highly aggressive.

“It’s a specific pathology feature that tends to indicate more aggressive behavior and that tends to be more common in younger patients,” Ng says. “Younger patients also have tumors more commonly in the left side of the colon and the rectum compared with older patients, and we don’t really understand why that is.”

Ng has mapped out every single cell in early-onset colorectal tumors so she can compare them with later-onset tumors to get more granular detail. The study was recently accepted for publication in *Nature Medicine*.

More research is needed to better clarify the molecular structure of these tumors before scientists can draw conclusions or shape treatments around them, says Cercek, who is continuing to chip away at these theories. “Maybe I’ll be able to tell you in a couple of years,” she adds.

Meanwhile researchers are pursuing a parallel line of inquiry: whether subtle, chronic changes in healthy colon tissue may set the stage for cancer to develop.

One day, while performing surgery on a young patient with colorectal cancer, Emina Huang noticed something strange about the colon tissue: it was firmer than typical healthy tissue.

“When I was in the operating room, I just wondered: Was I really feeling that the young people’s colons were stiffer? Was it my imagination?” recalls Huang, a surgical scientist who has been studying the genesis of colorectal cancer at the University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center.

Huang’s lab has been investigating the role of chronic gut inflammation in abnormal cell growth for more than two decades. Inflammation that goes unchecked by the immune system’s typical control measures has been strongly connected to various types of cancers; people with inflammatory bowel disease, for instance, appear to have an increased risk of developing colorectal cancer, for reasons that aren’t entirely clear, Huang says.

To validate what Huang noticed in the operating room, she and her team conducted a biomechanical study of colon tissue collected from 19 people aged 57 to 70 and 14 people aged 42 to 46 with stage II or III tumors. Describing the results in a recent paper in *Advanced Science*, the researchers said young people with colorectal cancer had stiffer tumors than older individuals. Even more striking, their normal, noncancerous tissues were also firmer than those of older patients with colorectal cancer.

Huang suggests the rigid tissue may arise from chronic inflammation that leads to fibrosis, or tissue scarring. This scarring “is the root of many types of evil, from high blood pressure to cardiac disease to kidney failure to liver failure,” she says. Instead of focusing on the immune cells needed to fight harmful pathogens that are typically involved in temporary inflammation, her team focused on fibroblasts—cells that make strands of collagen, a protein that supports tissue structure. Under scarring conditions, collagen is more abundant and has a different arrangement.

“What we found is that the collagen in these \[younger\] patients is thicker, and it’s more aligned, instead of being like a crisscross network,” Huang says. Similar to strands of dried spaghetti, the collagen is more linear, she says, which makes it “easier for the cancer cells to crawl and move.”

Activation of specific collagen-producing fibroblasts could prime tissues to become ideal environments for cancerous spread, the findings suggest. Additional genetic analysis of the samples revealed higher expression of genes linked to collagen metabolism, blood vessel formation and inflammation in cancer tissues from young individuals compared with those of older patients.

These kinds of data could lead to new treatments, such as therapies to tamp down colorectal cancer–related inflammation or stop fibrosis, Huang says. They also could open up possibilities for preventive screening tests that are less invasive than the current most common approach, colonoscopy. Huang has concepts in mind for a noninvasive tissue stiffness test but says the work is still in very early stages.

When Cheatem received his diagnosis, he was 42—three years younger than the age at which people in the U.S. without a family history of colorectal cancer are advised to start screening for the illness. His tumor was right on the border between stages II and III. If clinicians had caught it at stage II, he wouldn’t have needed chemotherapy, which came with a host of side effects that interfered with his life and work.

On his “off” weeks, when Cheatem wasn’t getting an infusion of chemo, he could work, eat and exercise more normally. But as treatment progressed, his “off” weeks started to resemble his “on” weeks: he’d be overcome with nausea, exhaustion and persistent sensitivity to cold. “Because my chemotherapy was in the winter, I had gloves on, like, pretty much all hours of the day because of the pain attributed to the cold sensitivity,” he says. “Touching something cold was more like sticking your finger in a socket.”

Colorectal cancer and its treatments can be incredibly demanding regardless of a person’s age, but younger individuals can experience additional burdens. “They’re in the midst of their careers. Some of the very youngest ones are still in the midst of their education,” Ng says. Many people need to work to stay on health insurance, and many are caregivers themselves—80 percent of people with early-onset colorectal cancer have children under the age of 18 when diagnosed. For those who plan to have more children, treatments can negatively affect fertility, Ng adds.

Both her center and Cercek’s clinic for young-onset colorectal cancer offer psychological and social support to improve the quality of life of people who are recovering from the disease. Their teams are also testing therapies that minimize toxicity from treatment—but finding colorectal cancer early has always been directly tied to better health outcomes.

Experts attribute the decline in mortality from the disease among older adults to screening and early detection. The younger age groups experiencing the sharpest rise in rates aren’t included in the current screening recommendations.

Earlier screening could help untangle some of these questions. But it’s difficult, with the current evidence, to argue for screening people at younger and younger ages—particularly if the growth of colorectal cancer potentially starts in childhood or adolescence.

“We have to prove that there really is enough reason to make that recommendation to a 15-year-old or a 20-year-old,” Jaffee says. She adds that health disparities already prevent many people who are eligible from getting screened, and insurance doesn’t always cover screening.

Colonoscopy is considered the most accurate available screening option—and clinicians can remove precancerous polyps while doing the exam—but the procedure is invasive and almost always requires sedation and intensive bowel prep. More accessible tests could make it easier to screen people earlier. At-home stool tests—such as Cologuard and others that detect cancer-linked DNA markers or blood in stool—can help provide initial assessments to determine whether someone should get further follow-up diagnostic procedures, Jaffee says. A blood test for colon cancer has been approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration and was recently recommended by the American Cancer Society, although the USPSTF has not endorsed it because it’s shown to be less effective at catching very early-stage cancers. Jaffee says more advanced, accurate blood tests could be a cheaper first-step screening option for young individuals without known risk factors. Such tests might have caught Cheatem’s cancer at an earlier stage.

Painting has helped Cheatem manage the physical and emotional toll of cancer during and even after his treatment, he says. After he entered remission, he was inspired to create an art exhibition of self-portraits and important objects that reflected his experience. One piece from the series stands out to him now: a photorealistic painting of sliced and squeezed limes paired with a bunch of green grapes.

During chemotherapy, when Cheatem’s nausea would wreak havoc, he could stomach only green grapes and warm water with a squeeze of lime juice. Those fruits, he says, remain symbols of relief—a reminder of the “magic combination” that kept him going.

\**Editor’s Note (11/19/26): This sentence was edited after posting to correct the description of Kimmie Ng’s comment.*

On “about my fourth trip to the ER and my fourth CT \[computed tomography\] scan, a specialist said there was no way that \[this\] was diverticulitis,” Cheatem says. “It was something further.”
Doctors found an advanced malignant tumor in Cheatem’s lower colon. That September, at age 42, he was diagnosed with stage III colorectal cancer, which set him on a path to surgery and chemotherapy.

He was completely thrown by the words coming out of the doctor’s mouth. Cheatem thought he was healthy; he ate healthily and exercised regularly, and in his artwork he even avoided using oil-based paints known to contain carcinogens. Plus, he had no family history of colorectal cancer. “The cancer diagnosis itself came as a shock because I felt like I had been taking so many steps to simply not get cancer,” says Cheatem, who now lives in Texas.

Stories like Cheatem’s are becoming more common as severe colorectal cancer rates rise among younger, traditionally low-risk people. And these cases have grown increasingly visible. Actors James Van Der Beek and Chadwick Boseman were both in their 40s when they died from the disease. The uptick in cases has some scientists wondering whether they’re dealing with an entirely new type of colorectal cancer. As they race to find clues to explain the disturbing trend, several theories are emerging.

Colorectal cancer is still far more common in adults older than age 65. What’s shifted is the frequency of cases: the rate among older adults has been declining, but the number of diagnoses in younger people has continued to escalate since the mid-1990s. In response to the trend, in 2021, the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) lowered the recommended screening age from 50 to 45. In January 2026, the American Cancer Society’s annual report stated that colorectal cancer had officially become the deadliest cancer in people under age 50 in the U.S. Similar increases in rates of the cancer in younger age groups have been seen globally. People born in the 1990s have at least a fourfold-higher risk of developing colorectal cancer than those born in the 1960s in countries such as Australia, Canada and England. Health registries in Korea, Japan, Thailand and India have also reported increasing cases over the past several decades. Epidemiologists have noticed that the spike in incidence is tied to the time when a person was born, pointing toward generational shifts in risk or exposure.
“Is this a completely new cancer that we’re now seeing in young people for whatever reason?” —Andrea Cercek *Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center*

Most experts agree that the cause or causes won’t be clear-cut. Family history and genetics have been strongly associated with higher risk. But Kimmie Ng, an oncologist and leader in early-onset colorectal cancer research, and her team at the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute have seen not only an overall surge in cases in young people but more advanced-stage tumors in people who have no family history of cancer and are otherwise in good health, similar to Cheatem. Some research suggests that generational shifts in lifestyle, such as eating more processed foods and getting less physical activity, and environmental factors—including exposure to plastics and toxic chemicals—probably play some role.

Unknown exposures in childhood or even in the womb could be factors, Ng says. Delays in getting tested may also explain part of it, she adds. A 2018 report found that 67 percent of people diagnosed with early-onset colorectal cancer went to at least two physicians before receiving that diagnosis. Ng suspects, however, that there is more to the mysterious trend. “Regardless of how they were diagnosed, the survival of the very youngest patients is still worse,” she says. “That suggests to me that there may be something biologically different.”

Johns Hopkins University oncologist Elizabeth Jaffee agrees that delays in diagnosis go only so far toward explaining the surge. “We don’t know what’s driving these \[tumors\] biologically yet, and that’s really the problem,” she says. “We need more biology to go along with all of this epidemiology and correlative studies.”

Every year, leading cancer experts flock to one of the biggest meetings in their field—the American Association of Cancer Research’s annual meeting. And increasingly, the phenomenon of early-onset colorectal cancer is a major topic of conversation. At the 2025 conference, Jaffee moderated a panel focused on the challenges facing colorectal cancer researchers and patients. Panelist and oncologist Andrea Cercek posed a query that has continued to weigh heavily on researchers and clinicians.

“Is this a completely new cancer that we’re now seeing in young people for whatever reason?” asked Cercek, co-director of the Center for Young Onset Colorectal and Gastrointestinal Cancer at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center. “Or \[has there\] just been this shift that’s now happening younger and younger?”

Cancer can be a slow, surreptitious illness—for decades researchers have called it a “disease of the aging.” Cells constantly turn over, and little mistakes—or mutations—can sneak into new batches. The body usually catches and eliminates these faulty cells, but with age, that process can slow down, and abnormal cells can pile up. “Mutation after mutation happens, and then it turns into a carcinoma,” Cercek told me.

Colorectal cancer typically follows a 10- to 15-year timeline from normal cell to small growth or polyp to, eventually, a larger mass or tumor. If mutant cells are not detected, they may amass over decades in older adults. Cercek and other researchers are investigating whether something might accelerate the timeline in people who develop the disease at a younger age.

Genetically, colorectal tumors look surprisingly similar in young and old bodies, involving roughly the same groups of mutations. In 2021 Cercek’s team found that tumors from people as young as age 14 and as old as age 93 showed no significant genetic differences. But how those mutations occur in the first place could explain why the tumors pop up earlier in some people.

“Babies or young kids or adolescents \[could be\] exposed to something in the environment that leads to some biological changes early in life that then predispose them to the development of cancer at a younger age than we have historically seen,” says Ng, who leads the Young-Onset Colorectal Cancer Center at Dana-Farber. “I do think that it is key to try to study early-life factors, though it’s really hard to do.”

Ng helped to create the center in 2019 to address the trend head-on, launching research that has involved collecting various samples, including blood, stool and tumor tissue, from patients under age 50 treated at Dana-Farber. The data gathered over time might reveal links between tumor mutations and the gut microbiome.

A different team solidified an important lead in 2025: in data collected from 11 countries on four continents, the researchers identified two peculiar patterns of DNA, or mutational signatures, whose prevalence was more than three times higher among people under age 40 with colorectal cancer than among people age 70 and older who also had the disease. These mutational signatures can tell doctors what jump-started the chain of events that led to the cancerous tumor.

The researchers suggest that the two mutational signatures are linked to a toxin called colibactin, which is produced by gut bacteria such as *Escherichia coli* that contain genes encoding polyketide synthase enzymes, called *pks*-positive bacteria. The toxin might damage DNA in healthy colon crypts—tubelike mucus glands that line the colon and rectum—potentially prompting tumor growth.

“Modeling investigations seem to find that \[*pks*-positive *E. coli*\] colonize very, very young individuals, probably in the first decade of life,” says Ng, who was not involved in the study.\* “One of the hypotheses is that perhaps \[some\] young children are colonized with *pks*-positive *E. coli*.” Past evidence has found high levels of *pks-positive E. coli in infants* without any associated negative health effects or higher risk of cancer. But Ng says further research studies are needed to determine the extent of *pks*-positive bacteria in children and the possible effects on health outcomes.

A group of researchers, including Ng’s team, plans to confirm these findings in a larger population in the U.S. and elsewhere. The scientists are also aiming to better understand the prevalence of *pks*-positive *E. coli* in children.

When Ng looks through her microscope at young patients’ tissue samples, she tries to coax stories out of the tumors—little signs of their progression and characteristics. Are there certain molecular traits that make some tumors spread faster or more aggressively than others?

For instance, Ng’s and Cercek’s teams have independently found that people who are younger than age 35 when they’re diagnosed with colon cancer tend to die more quickly than any other age group. People in their 20s and 30s, groups where the rates are rising most steeply, have the worst survival outcomes—even compared with patients in their 60s, Ng says.

Under the microscope, younger individuals’ tumor cells can appear more disorganized and abnormal compared with healthy tissue, Ng explains. Past research has shown that early-onset colorectal cancers in patients under age 40 also have higher rates of signet ring cell carcinoma—a type of cancer that is highly aggressive.

“It’s a specific pathology feature that tends to indicate more aggressive behavior and that tends to be more common in younger patients,” Ng says. “Younger patients also have tumors more commonly in the left side of the colon and the rectum compared with older patients, and we don’t really understand why that is.”

Ng has mapped out every single cell in early-onset colorectal tumors so she can compare them with later-onset tumors to get more granular detail. The study was recently accepted for publication in *Nature Medicine*.

More research is needed to better clarify the molecular structure of these tumors before scientists can draw conclusions or shape treatments around them, says Cercek, who is continuing to chip away at these theories. “Maybe I’ll be able to tell you in a couple of years,” she adds.
Meanwhile researchers are pursuing a parallel line of inquiry: whether subtle, chronic changes in healthy colon tissue may set the stage for cancer to develop.
One day, while performing surgery on a young patient with colorectal cancer, Emina Huang noticed something strange about the colon tissue: it was firmer than typical healthy tissue.

“When I was in the operating room, I just wondered: Was I really feeling that the young people’s colons were stiffer? Was it my imagination?” recalls Huang, a surgical scientist who has been studying the genesis of colorectal cancer at the University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center.

Huang’s lab has been investigating the role of chronic gut inflammation in abnormal cell growth for more than two decades. Inflammation that goes unchecked by the immune system’s typical control measures has been strongly connected to various types of cancers; people with inflammatory bowel disease, for instance, appear to have an increased risk of developing colorectal cancer, for reasons that aren’t entirely clear, Huang says.

To validate what Huang noticed in the operating room, she and her team conducted a biomechanical study of colon tissue collected from 19 people aged 57 to 70 and 14 people aged 42 to 46 with stage II or III tumors. Describing the results in a recent paper in *Advanced Science*, the researchers said young people with colorectal cancer had stiffer tumors than older individuals. Even more striking, their normal, noncancerous tissues were also firmer than those of older patients with colorectal cancer.

Huang suggests the rigid tissue may arise from chronic inflammation that leads to fibrosis, or tissue scarring. This scarring “is the root of many types of evil, from high blood pressure to cardiac disease to kidney failure to liver failure,” she says. Instead of focusing on the immune cells needed to fight harmful pathogens that are typically involved in temporary inflammation, her team focused on fibroblasts—cells that make strands of collagen, a protein that supports tissue structure. Under scarring conditions, collagen is more abundant and has a different arrangement.

“What we found is that the collagen in these \[younger\] patients is thicker, and it’s more aligned, instead of being like a crisscross network,” Huang says. Similar to strands of dried spaghetti, the collagen is more linear, she says, which makes it “easier for the cancer cells to crawl and move.”

Activation of specific collagen-producing fibroblasts could prime tissues to become ideal environments for cancerous spread, the findings suggest. Additional genetic analysis of the samples revealed higher expression of genes linked to collagen metabolism, blood vessel formation and inflammation in cancer tissues from young individuals compared with those of older patients.

These kinds of data could lead to new treatments, such as therapies to tamp down colorectal cancer–related inflammation or stop fibrosis, Huang says. They also could open up possibilities for preventive screening tests that are less invasive than the current most common approach, colonoscopy. Huang has concepts in mind for a noninvasive tissue stiffness test but says the work is still in very early stages.

When Cheatem received his diagnosis, he was 42—three years younger than the age at which people in the U.S. without a family history of colorectal cancer are advised to start screening for the illness. His tumor was right on the border between stages II and III. If clinicians had caught it at stage II, he wouldn’t have needed chemotherapy, which came with a host of side effects that interfered with his life and work.

On his “off” weeks, when Cheatem wasn’t getting an infusion of chemo, he could work, eat and exercise more normally. But as treatment progressed, his “off” weeks started to resemble his “on” weeks: he’d be overcome with nausea, exhaustion and persistent sensitivity to cold. “Because my chemotherapy was in the winter, I had gloves on, like, pretty much all hours of the day because of the pain attributed to the cold sensitivity,” he says. “Touching something cold was more like sticking your finger in a socket.”

Colorectal cancer and its treatments can be incredibly demanding regardless of a person’s age, but younger individuals can experience additional burdens. “They’re in the midst of their careers. Some of the very youngest ones are still in the midst of their education,” Ng says. Many people need to work to stay on health insurance, and many are caregivers themselves—80 percent of people with early-onset colorectal cancer have children under the age of 18 when diagnosed. For those who plan to have more children, treatments can negatively affect fertility, Ng adds.

Both her center and Cercek’s clinic for young-onset colorectal cancer offer psychological and social support to improve the quality of life of people who are recovering from the disease. Their teams are also testing therapies that minimize toxicity from treatment—but finding colorectal cancer early has always been directly tied to better health outcomes.

Experts attribute the decline in mortality from the disease among older adults to screening and early detection. The younger age groups experiencing the sharpest rise in rates aren’t included in the current screening recommendations.

Earlier screening could help untangle some of these questions. But it’s difficult, with the current evidence, to argue for screening people at younger and younger ages—particularly if the growth of colorectal cancer potentially starts in childhood or adolescence.

“We have to prove that there really is enough reason to make that recommendation to a 15-year-old or a 20-year-old,” Jaffee says. She adds that health disparities already prevent many people who are eligible from getting screened, and insurance doesn’t always cover screening.

Colonoscopy is considered the most accurate available screening option—and clinicians can remove precancerous polyps while doing the exam—but the procedure is invasive and almost always requires sedation and intensive bowel prep. More accessible tests could make it easier to screen people earlier. At-home stool tests—such as Cologuard and others that detect cancer-linked DNA markers or blood in stool—can help provide initial assessments to determine whether someone should get further follow-up diagnostic procedures, Jaffee says. A blood test for colon cancer has been approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration and was recently recommended by the American Cancer Society, although the USPSTF has not endorsed it because it’s shown to be less effective at catching very early-stage cancers. Jaffee says more advanced, accurate blood tests could be a cheaper first-step screening option for young individuals without known risk factors. Such tests might have caught Cheatem’s cancer at an earlier stage.

Painting has helped Cheatem manage the physical and emotional toll of cancer during and even after his treatment, he says. After he entered remission, he was inspired to create an art exhibition of self-portraits and important objects that reflected his experience. One piece from the series stands out to him now: a photorealistic painting of sliced and squeezed limes paired with a bunch of green grapes.

During chemotherapy, when Cheatem’s nausea would wreak havoc, he could stomach only green grapes and warm water with a squeeze of lime juice. Those fruits, he says, remain symbols of relief—a reminder of the “magic combination” that kept him going.
